Below is a verse‑by‑verse commentary on Joshua 15:43–63, drawn from the websites you permitted. Where a source was reached through a summary page, the URL of that page is given; where a link went directly to the commentary, the specific URL is provided.

---

## Verses 43–44: The Southern Shephelah Group

**v. 43: Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib**

These three towns belong to the fourth group in the Shephelah (lowland), a list of nine cities (v. 44). The Shephelah was the rolling hill country between the coastal plain and the central mountains of Judah.

- **Nezib** is identified by the 19th‑century geographer Dr. Edward Robinson and J. L. Porter with the ruins of *Beit Nusib*, about seven miles east of Eleutheropolis (Beit‑Jibrin), on the way to Hebron. Porter describes it: “It is neither in the mountains nor in the plain, but in the low hilly country which connects the two. The ruins are of considerable extent. The most important are a massive tower sixty feet square, the masonry of which appears to be of the Jewish type.” (Whedon’s Commentary, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-15.html

- **Iphtah** and **Ashnah** (not the same Ashnah as in v. 33) are largely unknown; Keil & Delitzsch note that this group belongs to “the towns of the lowland or shephelah” and that the fourth group consists of towns “in the southern part of the shephelah.” (Keil & Delitzsch, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

**v. 44: Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah—nine cities, along with their villages.**

- **Keilah** is a well‑known walled town. David rescued it from the Philistines (1 Sam 23:1–13) and later had to flee when its inhabitants planned to hand him over to Saul. Jerome records it as a village about eight Roman miles east of Eleutheropolis on the road to Hebron, where the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk was shown. Later it appears in Nehemiah 3:17. (Gill’s Exposition; Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary via biblehub.com)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-15.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-44.htm

- **Achzib** is probably identical with *Chezib* (Gen 38:5) and is preserved in the ruins at *Kussbeh* (or *Kesba*), about five hours south‑west of Beit‑Jibrin. (Keil & Delitzsch, via biblehub.com)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-44.htm

- **Mareshah** (also Maresheth, Marasthi) was fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chr 11:8). It was the site of Asa’s great victory over Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chr 14:9–15), the birthplace of the prophet Micah (Mic 1:1,14–15), and the home of Eliezer (2 Chr 20:37). In the inter‑testamental period it was the important town of *Marissa*. Robinson identifies it with the ruins called *Marash*, about 1½ miles south of Beit‑Jibrin. (Whedon; Gill; Pulpit Commentary)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-15.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-44.htm

## Verses 45–47: The Philistine Coastal Cities

**v. 45: Ekron, with its towns and villages**

Ekron was one of the five Philistine capital cities (the northernmost). Though allotted to Judah here, it was later assigned to Dan (Josh 19:43) and “remained almost entirely in the hands of the Philistines” throughout the Old Testament period. It was to Ekron that the ark was taken after the battle of Aphek (1 Sam 5:10). (Keil & Delitzsch; Ellicott)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html

**v. 46: from Ekron to the sea, all the cities near Ashdod, along with their villages**

This verse describes the coastal strip west of Ekron down to the Mediterranean. The text does not name individual towns in this stretch, because, as Keil notes, “Judah never actually obtained possession of them.” The allotment was made by divine command even for territory not yet conquered (cf. Josh 13:6). (Keil & Delitzsch)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

**v. 47: Ashdod … Gaza … as far as the Brook of Egypt and the coastline of the Great Sea.**

- **Ashdod** (modern *Esdûd*) and **Gaza** (modern *Ghuzzeh*) were two more Philistine principalities. Gaza was the southernmost, near the coast.
- **Gath** and **Ashkelon** are not named, but Keil explains they were “included in the boundaries named.” Ashkelon lay between Ashdod and Gaza on the coast; Gath lay to the east of Ekron and Ashdod. (Keil & Delitzsch)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html
- The “Brook of Egypt” (*Wady el‑Arish*) formed the southern boundary (cf. Josh 15:4). The “coastline of the Great Sea” marked the western limit.
- This entire Philistine strip, though allotted to Judah, was never fully possessed by the tribe in the period before the monarchy. The Expositor’s Bible notes that these cities “of the Philistines” were “aggregated, because they were not conquered.” (Whedon)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-15.html

## Verses 48–51: The First Group in the Hill Country (South‑West)

**v. 48: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh**

With v. 48 the scene shifts from the Shephelah to “the hill country” (mountains of Judah). The mountains rise to about 3,000 feet near Hebron, are limestone, rugged but intersected by fertile valleys, and were “thickly covered with towns” in antiquity. (Keil & Delitzsch)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

- **Shamir** is thought to be preserved in the ruins of *Um Shaumerah* (Robinson).  
- **Jattir** was a priestly city (Josh 21:14), mentioned also in 1 Sam 30:27; identified with ruins at *Attir*.  
- **Socoh** is the present *Shuweikeh*, about two hours north‑west of Jattir. (Keil & Delitzsch; Barnes)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/joshua/15.htm

**v. 49: Dannah, Kiriath‑sannah (that is, Debir)**

- **Dannah** is unknown; most commentators say it has not been identified.
- **Kiriath‑sannah** = **Debir**. The name means “city of the palm” (sannah). It is the same Debir (also called Kiriath‑sepher, “city of books”) that was conquered by Joshua (Josh 10:38–39) and later taken by Othniel at Caleb’s challenge (Josh 15:15–17). Its exact site is uncertain, though some link it to *Dewir‑ban* west of Hebron. (Ellicott; Keil)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

**v. 50: Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim**

- **Anab**: A city whose Anakim inhabitants were “cut off” by Joshua (Josh 11:21).  
- **Eshtemoh** (or Eshtemoa): A Levitical city (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57), now *Semua*, an inhabited village east of Socoh with ancient walls and a castle of ancient date. It is also where David sent spoils (1 Sam 30:28).  
- **Anim**: Possibly contracted from *Ayanim* (“fountains”), preserved in the ruins of *el Ghuwein* south of Semua. (Keil & Delitzsch)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

**v. 51: Goshen, Holon, and Giloh—eleven cities**

- **Goshen**: Not the same as the land of Goshen in Egypt. Keil and others consider the “land of Goshen” in Josh 10:41 to be a separate region. The town itself is unknown.  
- **Holon**: Another priestly city (Josh 21:15).  
- **Giloh**: The birthplace of Ahithophel, David’s counsellor who betrayed him (2 Sam 15:12). (Ellicott; Keil)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

## Verses 52–54: The Second Hill‑Country Group (Near Hebron)

**v. 52: Arab, Dumah, Eshan**
**v. 53: Janim, Beth‑tappuah, Aphekah**
**v. 54: Humtah, Kiriath‑arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior—nine cities**

- **Kiriath‑arba (Hebron)** is the most significant. It was the city of Arba, “the greatest man among the Anakim” (Josh 14:15), given to Caleb as his inheritance. It later became one of the cities of refuge and a Levitical city, and it served as David’s capital for his first seven years as king (2 Sam 2:1–4).  
- The other towns in this group are mostly unidentified, except **Beth‑tappuah** (“house of apples”), which may be the modern *Teffuh*, west of Hebron.  
- Dr. Constable notes that this group of nine stood “to the north” of the first group, “near Hebron.” (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-15.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

## Verses 55–57: The Third Hill‑Country Group (Eastward Toward the Wilderness)

**v. 55: Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah**
**v. 56: Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah**
**v. 57: Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah—ten cities**

- **Maon, Carmel, and Ziph** are especially famous from the story of David’s flight from Saul. Maon was the home of Nabal and Abigail (1 Sam 25); the wilderness of Ziph is where the Ziphites twice betrayed David to Saul (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1). (Barnes; Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/joshua/15.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html

- **Carmel** here is not Mount Carmel on the coast, but a town in the Judean hill country near Maon, also associated with Nabal and Abigail.  
- **Juttah**: A priestly city (Josh 21:16), traditionally the hometown of Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:39–40, though Luke calls it “a town in the hill country of Judah”).  
- **Jezreel**: Not the northern Jezreel of the valley of that name, but a southern town. Its location is uncertain.  
- **Gibeah**: Not to be confused with Gibeah of Benjamin (Saul’s hometown). This is a southern Gibeah in Judah.  
- **Timnah**: Noted as the place where Judah sheared his sheep (Gen 38:12–14). (Ellicott; Barnes)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/joshua/15.htm

- The Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary notes that these ten cities “were later the haunt of David in his flight from Saul, in the far south beyond Beer‑sheba (1 Samuel chapters 25–26).” (Garner‑Howes, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-15.html

## Verses 58–59: The Fourth Hill‑Country Group (North of Hebron)

**v. 58: Halhul, Beth‑zur, Gedor**
**v. 59: Maarath, Beth‑anoth, and Eltekon—six cities**

- **Halhul** is identified with modern *Halhul*, a village north of Hebron on the road to Jerusalem, near the traditional site of the tombs of the prophets Gad and Nathan.  
- **Beth‑zur** (“house of rock”) was fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chr 11:7) and was an important Maccabean fortress (1 Macc 4:61; 6:7). It sits on a hill north of Hebron.  
- **Gedor**, **Maarath**, **Beth‑anoth**, and **Eltekon** are mostly unidentified. Five of the six have been tentatively identified by Conder’s survey. (Ellicott)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html

**A significant textual note on the missing group in the Hebrew text:** Between v. 59 and v. 60, the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament) preserves a fifth group of eleven towns that is absent from the Masoretic (Hebrew) text. Keil & Delitzsch explain that “an ancient copyist passed by mistake from the word וחצריהן in Joshua 15:59 to the same word at the close of the missing section.” The LXX lists: *Tekoa, Ephratah (that is, Bethlehem), Phagor, Aetan (Etam), Kulon, Tatam, Thobes (or Sores), Karem, Galem, Thether (or Baither), and Mamocho* — eleven cities. This includes **Bethlehem** (Ephratah), the birthplace of Christ, and **Tekoa**, the home of Amos. (Keil & Delitzsch)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

## Verse 60: The Last Hill‑Country Group (Northern Border)

**v. 60: Kiriath‑baal (that is, Kiriath‑jearim), and Rabbah—two cities**

- **Kiriath‑baal / Kiriath‑jearim** (“city of Baal” / “city of forests”): This was one of the Gibeonite cities (Josh 9:17) and later the place where the ark of the covenant resided for 20 years after being returned by the Philistines (1 Sam 7:1–2). Conder identifies it with *’Arma* (or *’Erma*), about four miles east of Beth‑shemesh. It lay on the northern border of Judah, near Benjamin. (Ellicott)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html

- **Rabbah**: Not the Ammonite capital, but a town in Judah, marked on the map as *Rubba* (Conder). (Ellicott)

- This group of only two cities represented Judah’s northernmost border. Dr. Constable describes these as “two on Judah’s northern border.” (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-15.html

## Verses 61–62: The Wilderness Cities

**v. 61: Beth‑arabah, Middin, Secacah**
**v. 62: Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En‑gedi—six cities**

The “wilderness” of Judah lies between the hill country and the Dead Sea. It is a “terrible desert, with a soil composed of chalk, marl, and limestone, and with bald mountains covered with flint and hornstone” (Keil & Delitzsch). Yet springs create pockets of lush vegetation. This region was the scene of David’s wanderings (1 Sam 23–24), the preaching of John the Baptist (Matt 3:1), and perhaps our Lord’s temptation (Matt 4).

- **Beth‑arabah**: “House of the Arabah/desert,” near the Dead Sea, on the border with Benjamin (Josh 15:6).  
- **Middin**: Possibly the ruins of *Mird* or *Mardeh*, west of the northern end of the Dead Sea.  
- **Secacah**: Identified with *Sikkkeh* in the same region. (Ellicott; Keil & Delitzsch)  
- **Nibshan**: Unknown.  
- **The City of Salt**: Not named elsewhere, but likely near the Dead Sea and the “Valley of Salt” (2 Sam 8:13; Ps 60 title). The Hebrew *‘ir hammelaḥ* connects it to the salt‑rich region.  
- **En‑gedi** (“spring of the kid”): A famous oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, where David hid from Saul in the caves (1 Sam 24). Still known as *Ain Jidy*, it is a lush spot with a perennial spring. (Barnes; Keil & Delitzsch; Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/joshua/15.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

## Verse 63: The Failure to Drive Out the Jebusites

**v. 63: “But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah.”**

This is the verse that receives the most theological attention across traditions.

### 1. The Historical Situation
Jerusalem sat on the border between Judah and Benjamin. The city (Jebus) was conquered in part during Joshua’s lifetime — the Israelites took and burned the “lower city” (Judg 1:8) — but the “upper city” (the stronghold of Zion) remained in Jebusite hands. Thus Jebusites “dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem” — a situation that lasted until David “took the stronghold of Zion” and made it his capital (2 Sam 5:6–9). (Ellicott; Barnes; Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-15.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-63.htm

### 2. Why “Could Not” Drive Them Out?

**The Reformed / Calvinist reading:** John Calvin insists that the phrase “could not” does **not** excuse Judah. It was not that God failed to give sufficient power — “had they exerted themselves to the full measure of their strength, and failed of success, the dishonor would have fallen on God himself, who had promised … to send hornets to drive out the inhabitants.” The real cause was “their own sluggishness,” “their neglect of the divine command from a love of ease.” Calvin adds a pointed application: “We ought to learn from it to make vigorous trial of our strength in attempting to accomplish the commands of God, and not to omit any opportunity, lest while we are idly resting the door may be shut.” He also notes that some Jewish expositors, “unwilling to admit the cowardice and sluggishness of their countrymen, fable that the Jebusites were permitted to remain … because they were descendants of Abimelech, and in consequence of the covenant made between him and Abraham … could not be lawfully expelled.” (Calvin’s Commentary, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-15.html

**Reformed / Ligonier:** Ligonier’s devotional notes that “Judah could not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem … which is interesting since Jerusalem was actually part of Benjamin’s territory.” The city was essentially on the border, so both tribes had a role. “Eventually, the city would be absorbed by Judah altogether.” (Ligonier)
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/territory-for-judah

**Baptist / Ironside:** H. A. Ironside calls this a “pathetic” failure: “tribe after tribe failed to make a full end of their enemies … compromise with evil never pays.” He notes that God had warned Israel that those not destroyed “would be thorns in their sides.” (Ironside’s Notes, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/joshua-15.html

**Baptist / Gray’s Concise Commentary:** “If Judah could not drive out the Jebusites it was not for lack of power, but faith. … All the sufferings of Israel for hundreds of years arose from that neglect.” (Gray, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/joshua-15.html

**The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary** (broadly Protestant homiletical tradition) outlines three steps: (1) “The inability which comes through unbelief” — God had promised victory, so the failure was due to distrust of God; (2) “Unbelief working fear and inaction” — when faith departs, fear enters and zeal departs; (3) “Fear and inaction resulting in continued shame and suffering” — Israel endured nearly four centuries of insult from the Jebusites, culminating in their taunt that even “the lame and the blind” could defend the walls (2 Sam 5:6). The work they failed to do at first “had to be done, after all.” (Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-15.html

**Enduring Word** (Pastor David Guzik, charismatic/Pentecostal tradition): “Jerusalem remained in Canaanite hands because Judah lacked the determination to finish the conquest, a reminder that God’s promises require our faith and effort, and excuses — no matter how reasonable — can block what He intends for us.” He adds that Jerusalem was “understandably a difficult city to conquer” because of its hilly terrain, “yet no matter how hard the struggle, with God’s promise and God’s help, God’s people can triumph.” (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**Keil & Delitzsch** (Lutheran/Conservative): The statement “applies to the interval between Joshua and David.” It “does not involve a contradiction” to Josh 18:28 or Judg 1:21, because “it is not said here that Jerusalem belonged to the tribe of Judah, or that the children of Judah alone had set up a claim to it.” (Keil & Delitzsch, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/joshua-15.html

### 3. The “To This Day” Clause and the Date of the Book

- **Clarke** argues that this verse proves the book of Joshua was “not written after the times of the Jewish kings,” because the Jebusites did not remain in Jerusalem after David expelled them. “Therefore the book was written before there were any kings in Judea.” (Clarke’s Commentary, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-15.html

- **The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary** makes the same point: the verse “still more emphatically claims to have been written prior to the time when David overcame the Jebusites.” (PHC, via studylight.org)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-15.html

### 4. Summary of Tradition‑Specific Emphases

All Protestant traditions reviewed here agree on the core reading: Judah’s failure was moral and spiritual (unbelief, sloth, love of ease), not a limitation of God’s power. The differences are in application:

- **Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier):** Emphasise God’s sovereignty and the inexcusability of human sloth — God had provided everything needed; the fault was entirely Judah’s.
- **Baptist (Ironside, Gray, Garner‑Howes):** Stress the danger of compromise with evil and the principle that incomplete obedience brings long‑term suffering.
- **Pentecostal/charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasize the necessity of faith and determination; God’s promises “require our faith and effort.”
- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Focus on the historical‑critical explanation, harmonizing the verse with Judges 1, without the strong moral exhortation of the other traditions.

No distinctively **Catholic, Orthodox, prosperity gospel, or hyper‑grace** readings of this verse were found in the search results from the approved sites. Neither newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, nor bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org appeared in the search returns for these verses.
